edbDesc: A fluid interface that can occur when there is velocity shear in a single continuous fluid, or where there is a velocity difference across the interface between two fluids. An example is wind blowing over water: The instability manifests in waves on the water surface. More generally, clouds, the ocean, Saturn's bands, and the sun's corona show this instability.
title: Kelvin-Helmholtz instability
description: When one layer of fluid slides over another, such as wind over water, the boundary rolls up into a row of curling waves; it's why some clouds look like a line of breaking surf. Helmholtz described it in 1868 and Lord Kelvin in 1871.
effect: a boundary between two fluids sliding past each other rolls up into waves
usedIn: Shear-layer mixing in jet-engine combustors and chemical mixers
strength: Any speed difference across a sharp boundary sets it growing; on a calm sea it takes a moderate breeze to raise waves this way.
pickWhy: Borderline: Specific and named, but it mostly explains things rather than driving inventions; kept since it does a job (mixing) and could do more.
